title: Vectors in W perpendicular to (w₁, w₂, w₃)

questions.prompt: What does it mean for v to be in W *and* perpendicular to w?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Two conditions: v is in W, and v ⊥ w. Step 2: This is an *intersection* of two subspaces. Step 3: The trap "random" misses the structure. Step 4: Used in *orthogonal projections*.

questions.prompt: Why is W ∩ w⊥ typically a *line*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W is 2D (a plane). Step 2: w⊥ is 1D (a line, perpendicular to w). Step 3: Their intersection is generically a line. Step 4: Used in *orthogonality*.

questions.prompt: What is the *orthogonal complement* of w?
questions.explanation: Step 1: w⊥ = {v : v · w = 0}. Step 2: All vectors perpendicular to w. Step 3: In ℝ³, w⊥ is 2D (a plane). Step 4: Used in *orthogonal complement theory*.

questions.prompt: Why is w⊥ in ℝ³ a *plane*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: w⊥ = {v : v · w = 0} — one linear equation. Step 2: One equation in 3 unknowns → 2D plane. Step 3: Used in Q3.4 connection.

questions.prompt: What is the *intersection* W ∩ w⊥ typically?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W is 2D. Step 2: w⊥ is 2D. Step 3: Two 2D subspaces in 3D generically intersect only at origin. Step 4: This is the *transverse intersection*. Step 5: Used in *orthogonality*.

questions.prompt: When is W ∩ w⊥ *more than just origin*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: If w ∈ W, the intersection W ∩ w⊥ is the direction in W perpendicular to w. Step 2: This is a line within W. Step 3: Used in *constrained subspaces*.

questions.prompt: What is the *null space* of the row space of W?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Row space of W = span of rows. Step 2: Null space of row space = vectors perpendicular to all rows. Step 3: This is the *orthogonal complement* of the row space. Step 4: Used in Q3.10.

questions.prompt: How is W ∩ w⊥ *computed*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Solve v ∈ W (parametrise as α(1,2,1) + β(2,7,3)). Step 2: And v ⊥ w (so v · w = 0). Step 3: Combine to get α, β. Step 4: Used in *constrained optimisation*.

questions.prompt: Why is W ∩ w⊥ *always* containing origin?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W (being a subspace) contains origin. Step 2: w⊥ (being a subspace) contains origin. Step 3: So intersection contains origin. Step 4: Used in *subspace theory*.

questions.prompt: What does *orthogonal complement* of W mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W⊥ = {v : v · w = 0 for all w ∈ W}. Step 2: All vectors perpendicular to every vector in W. Step 3: In ℝ³, if W is 2D plane, W⊥ is 1D line (normal). Step 4: Used in *orthogonal projection*.

questions.prompt: Why is dim(W) + dim(W⊥) = n?
questions.explanation: Step 1: For W a subspace of ℝⁿ: dim(W) + dim(W⊥) = n. Step 2: This is the *dimension theorem for orthogonal complements*. Step 3: For 2D W in ℝ³: 2 + 1 = 3. ✓ Step 4: Used in *Projection theory*.

questions.prompt: What is W⊥ if W = span{(1, 2, 1), (2, 7, 3)}?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W is 2D (plane). Step 2: W⊥ in ℝ³ is 3 − 2 = 1D (line). Step 3: This line is perpendicular to W. Step 4: The line is the *normal direction* to W. Step 5: Used in *3D graphics*.

questions.prompt: Is W *orthogonal* to W⊥?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W⊥ is defined as vectors perpendicular to W. Step 2: So W and W⊥ are orthogonal. Step 3: This is the *orthogonality of complementary subspaces*. Step 4: Used in *least squares*.

questions.prompt: What does v ⊥ W *mean*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: v · w = 0 for every w ∈ W. Step 2: v is perpendicular to the whole subspace. Step 3: This is the *full perpendicularity* definition. Step 4: Used in *orthogonal complement*.

questions.prompt: How is the *normal* to W related to W⊥?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The normal to W is perpendicular to W. Step 2: So normal ∈ W⊥. Step 3: In ℝ³, W⊥ is 1D = normal direction. Step 4: So they coincide. Step 5: Used in *3D geometry*.

questions.prompt: Why is W⊥ a *subspace*?
questions.explanation: Step 1: If v, u ∈ W⊥, then (v + u) · w = v · w + u · w = 0. So v + u ∈ W⊥. Step 2: Similarly for scaling. Step 3: Contains origin. Step 4: So W⊥ is a subspace. Step 5: Used in *subspace theory*.

questions.prompt: Is every vector in ℝ³ in W or W⊥?
questions.explanation: Step 1: ℝ³ = W ⊕ W⊥ (every vector = sum of components in W and W⊥). Step 2: This is the *direct sum decomposition*. Step 3: Every v has v_W ∈ W and v_N ∈ W⊥ with v = v_W + v_N. Step 4: Used in *projection*.

questions.prompt: What if W = ℝ³ (the whole space) — what is W⊥?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W = ℝ³ means every vector is in W. Step 2: W⊥ = {v : v ⊥ all of ℝ³} = only v = 0. Step 3: So W⊥ = {0}. Step 4: This "whole space perp = origin" is the extreme case.

questions.prompt: What if W = {0} (only origin) — what is W⊥?
questions.explanation: Step 1: W = {0}. Step 2: W⊥ = {v : v · 0 = 0} = all vectors. Step 3: So W⊥ = ℝ³. Step 4: This "trivial subspace perp = everything" is the other extreme. Step 5: Used in *extreme cases*.

questions.prompt: What if W = W⊥ — when is this possible?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: If W = W⊥, then every vector in W is perpendicular to itself. Step 2: Only zero vector has this property. Step 3: So W = W⊥ implies W = {0}. Step 4: This "self-perp = trivial" is a basic theorem.
